_comment: Cutout puppet breakdown of the approved hero sprite, for tools/split_parts.ps1.
`rect`  [x0, y0, x1, y1], normalised against the SOURCE image. Boxes may and
should overlap -- a shoulder belongs to both the torso and the arm, and
overlap is what hides the seam when the arm rotates.
`pivot` [x, y] normalised against the SOURCE image, not the box. This is the
joint the part rotates about: the shoulder for an arm, the hip for a
leg, the base of the neck for the head. Authored in source space
because that is the only frame a human can see the joint in.
`parent`/`z` describe the rig: what this part hangs off, and paint order
(higher z draws in front).
Numbers below were read off art/_preview/kid_grid.png. Adjust them by eye
against art/_preview/parts_debug.png -- run split_parts.ps1 -DebugOverlay and
check every cross lands on an actual joint. A pivot in the middle of a bicep
makes the arm swing like a broken wing, and it is not recoverable later.
The backpack tank is deliberately part of the torso rather than its own part:
it is strapped on, it never moves independently, and splitting it would buy
a seam for nothing. That is why the torso box reaches up to y 0.09 and out to
x 0.97 -- the tank's tip sticks up past the shoulder line, and at the earlier
y 0.26 / x 0.94 it belonged to no part at all and vanished from the rig. It
overlaps the head box, which costs nothing because the head draws in front.
Check every change with the reassembly test, not by eye on the boxes: compose
the parts back at their anchors and diff against the source. A part nobody
owns does not look wrong in the debug overlay -- it is simply absent.
`erase` on the torso is not optional. A box wide enough to hold the chest also
holds the head, both arms and both thighs, and those baked-in copies never
move -- so a rotating arm slides out from behind a second arm still standing
at rest. The four rects cut away, in order: the head, the left arm, the right
arm, and everything below the hips.
Each erase begins just BELOW the joint it relates to (arms at y 0.375/0.395,
legs at 0.700) so the shoulder pads and hip tops stay with the moving part and
rotate with it. Cutting at the joint itself leaves a notch in the silhouette
the moment a limb swings away.
Keep the erases NARROW. They must clear the limb without eating the body: the
arms hang mostly outside the torso silhouette, so cutting in as far as the arm
BOX reaches (0.285 / 0.715) removes real chest. Erase rects and part rects are
not the same thing.
The optional 5th number is the REFILL direction -- which side to take donor
pixels from: 0 right, 1 left, 2 below, 3 above. Without it the cut stays a
hole, and the hole is visible the instant the limb swings away: raise the
scalpel arm to guard and you see straight through his chest. The refill smears
the nearest surviving pixel back across the cut, clipped to the original
silhouette, giving a slightly smudged but solid body edge that is only ever
seen with a limb out of the way.
The head cut has no refill on purpose: the head never moves far enough to
expose it, and smearing scalp colour down over the collar would be worse than
the hole it prevents.
_attachments_comment: Held weapons. Not cut from the sprite -- separate art parented to a hand,
because the arms swing a full 360 degrees to follow the aim and a weapon
painted into the arm texture could never do that.
`z`        NEGATIVE, so the weapon draws BEHIND its arm. This is what makes
it read as held: the fist covers the grip and only the blade or
the barrel sticks out past the fingers. Drawn in front, the
weapon lies on top of the glove and looks stuck to the hand
rather than in it -- no amount of nudging the grip point fixes
that, because the problem is paint order, not position.
`grip`     where the hand is, in SOURCE image coordinates, same convention
as a part's pivot. Put it ON THE FIST, at the very bottom of the
arm -- not at the wrist and not where the arm looks like it ends.
Both grips were originally about 0.05 too high, which reads as the
weapon floating just off the hand rather than being held. Check it
by rendering the grip as a marker over the assembled character; it
is not something you can judge from the numbers.
`pivot`    the point ON THE WEAPON that sits in the hand, normalised to the
weapon image. Roughly the middle of its handle.
`muzzle`   normalised point on the weapon where projectiles are born. Only
meaningful for the gun. The rig turns this into a Marker2D so
gameplay code never has to know the sprite's dimensions.
`rotation` radians, the angle the weapon is held at RELATIVE to its arm.
The art points RIGHT (+X) and the arms hang DOWN, so +PI/2 lays a
weapon flat along its arm -- that is what the syringe wants,
because the whole arm points where the player aims.
The scalpel does NOT want that. Its arm hangs at the kid's side,
and a blade laid along it points at his own legs; but raising the
arm enough to lift the blade flings the hand right out to the
side, because the arm is nearly half his height. So the blade is
mounted at -1.40 instead: the hand stays low at his hip and the
blade angles up across his front, at torso height.
Player reads this angle back off the node rather than assuming
+PI/2, so changing it here cannot silently throw the aim off by
the difference.
